Keep the task decomposition explicit (a plan the model updates) and the state outside the model (a scratchpad, a database) so a crash or restart is recoverable. Memory is retrieval over past interactions, with the same grounding rules.

Give agents the narrowest toolset that can do the job, run them with least privilege, gate destructive actions behind human confirmation, and trace every step. Evaluate agents on task success, cost and steps over a fixed task set, not on demos. Most business problems need a workflow with a couple of model calls, not an open-ended agent.

entries.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
entries.summary: MCP is an open protocol for exposing tools, resources and prompts to any compatible model client over stdio or HTTP.
entries.body:
An MCP server declares tools with JSON-Schema arguments, resources (readable data such as files or records) and prompt templates. A client (an IDE, a desktop assistant, an agent runtime) connects, lists capabilities, and calls tools; the transport is stdio for local processes or HTTP for remote servers. It replaces per-vendor plugin formats, so one server serves many clients. In Python, FastMCP turns typed functions into tools with a decorator.

Security is the server's job: authenticate the client, scope permissions, validate inputs, and treat everything from the model as untrusted. Log tool calls. A server that can read files and browse the web is an exfiltration path if a prompt injection reaches the model, so keep dangerous capabilities separate and confirmed.

entries.title: Prompt injection and LLM application security
entries.summary: Any text the model reads can try to give it orders; treat retrieved and tool-returned content as untrusted data and limit what the model can do.
entries.body:
Direct injection is a user telling the model to ignore its instructions; indirect injection hides instructions in a web page, a document, an email or a tool result the model reads later. The dangerous combination is untrusted input plus a capable tool: a poisoned document instructing the agent to email the customer list. No prompt fully prevents it, so layer defences: delimit and label data as data, keep secrets and dangerous tools away from the model, require human confirmation for actions with side effects, restrict what tools can reach (allowlists, read-only credentials), validate and sanitise tool outputs, and put injection cases in the eval suite.

Also cover the classics: rate limiting, authentication, tenant isolation in retrieval, and never rendering model output as HTML unescaped. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications is the checklist.

entries.title: PII, GDPR, data residency and tenant isolation
entries.summary: Know where every byte is processed, under what contract, for whom; redact early and isolate tenants inside the index.
entries.body:
Residency is a physical and legal fact: an EU-region endpoint under a data-processing agreement that excludes training on your data, or a model self-hosted on EU infrastructure. Ask the provider in writing about processing region, retention and training use. Redact personal data (names, ids, emails) at ingestion and in questions before anything else sees it; keep the mapping outside the model. Enforce tenant filters inside the vector query, derived from the authenticated session, never from user-supplied fields, and test cross-tenant questions in the eval suite.

A breach may trigger a 72-hour notification duty for the data controller; design the kill switch and the audit log before launch. Document the data flows in the architecture diagram; the auditor will ask.

entries.title: Evaluation: golden sets, metrics and regression gates
entries.summary: Turn quality into numbers on a fixed set of real cases and run them on every change; nothing else counts as evidence.
entries.body:
Build a golden set of 50 to 200 real inputs with expected outputs, including hard cases and ones the system should refuse; grow it from production failures. Score with exact match or F1 where the answer is a label or a value, retrieval recall@k where the target is a chunk, and a rubric (via humans or an LLM judge) where the answer is prose. Separate metrics for retrieval, faithfulness, helpfulness, abstention, latency and cost. Run it in CI on every prompt, model, chunking or index change and block regressions.

Offline evals predict; online metrics confirm: log user feedback, escalations and corrections, and sample production traffic into the golden set monthly. A change without an eval number is a guess.

entries.title: LLM-as-judge: useful, biased, calibrate it
entries.summary: A model can grade answers at scale, but it prefers long answers and the first option; use rubrics, swap positions, and check against humans.
entries.body:
Give the judge a rubric with explicit criteria and a scale, the question, the reference or the retrieved context, and the answer; ask for reasoning then a score in JSON. Known biases: verbosity (longer looks better), position (first of two wins), self-preference (a model likes its own style), and leniency. Mitigate with pairwise comparisons run in both orders, length-normalised scoring, a different model family as judge, and a human-labelled sample to measure agreement (Cohen's kappa) before trusting it. Re-calibrate when the judge model changes.

Use the judge for regression detection and triage, not as the sole acceptance criterion in a contract. Faithfulness judgments (is this claim supported by this chunk) are more reliable than open-ended quality scores.

entries.title: Regression suites, shadow deployments and A/B tests for LLM features
entries.summary: Gate changes on the offline suite, then roll out gradually and compare online metrics before committing.
entries.body:
Prompt, model and index changes go through the same path as code: the golden set runs in CI and a regression blocks the merge. Then shadow the new version on live traffic without showing users its output, comparing metrics and costs; then a canary to a small percentage with a kill switch; then an A/B test with enough traffic to detect the effect you care about (thumbs, escalations, task completion, cost per request). Keep versions pinned and logged with every response so an incident can be traced to a change.

Vendor models change under the same name; pin dated model versions where the API allows and re-run the suite when you move.

entries.title: Cost engineering for LLM systems
entries.summary: Cost is tokens times price per request times volume; attack input tokens first, then route by difficulty.
entries.body:
Compute cost per request as input_tokens x input_price + output_tokens x output_price, then multiply by monthly volume and put the arithmetic in the proposal. Input usually dominates, so: cache the stable prefix, retrieve fewer and better chunks, trim system prompts and history, and cap output. Then route: a small model or classifier handles the easy majority and escalates the rest (a cascade), evaluated on the golden set for quality at cost. Batch APIs cut price for non-interactive work. Self-hosting pays only at sustained volume with an ops team.

Dashboard cost per request by stage and alert on a 30 percent week-over-week rise; the usual causes are a raised k, a longer prompt, untrimmed history, or a cache that stopped hitting after a system-prompt edit.

entries.title: Latency engineering: time to first token, streaming and the tail
entries.summary: Break the request into stages, measure p95 per stage, stream to hide decode, and trim input to cut prefill.
entries.body:
Time to first token is dominated by queueing plus prefill, which scales with input length; total time adds decode, which scales with output length. Streaming changes what the user waits for from the last token to the first. Levers in rough order of cost: stream, shorten prompts and retrieved context, cap output, cache the prefix, run retrieval and other calls concurrently, pick a smaller or faster model, and only then bigger infrastructure. For self-hosted models, continuous batching (vLLM) trades per-request latency for throughput; tune for your traffic.

Measure at the client, per stage, as percentiles, and alert on p95 against the contract. A 6 s p95 is usually one slow stage, not a slow model.

entries.title: Self-hosting versus APIs: vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama and when each fits
entries.summary: APIs win on capability and simplicity; self-hosting wins on residency, control and cost at sustained volume, if you can run it.
entries.body:
Hosted APIs give the strongest models, no ops, and pay-per-token; the questions are data residency, retention and price at scale. Open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma) run on your hardware: vLLM for production throughput with continuous batching and prefix caching on GPUs; llama.cpp for CPU and quantised GGUF models on modest machines; Ollama for a developer-friendly local server with an OpenAI-compatible API. A 7B to 14B quantised model runs on a single consumer GPU and handles narrow tasks well; frontier-level quality still needs large models and serious hardware.

Decide with numbers: monthly token volume, required quality on the golden set, residency constraints, and the cost of an engineer who can keep GPUs healthy. Many teams run a hybrid: hosted for hard queries, self-hosted small models for classification and routing.

entries.title: Small models, distillation and quantisation
entries.summary: Shrink cost with a smaller model where quality allows: distil from a large one, quantise weights, and route by difficulty.
entries.body:
Distillation trains a small model on outputs (and sometimes reasoning) generated by a large one for your task, capturing most of the quality at a fraction of the cost. Quantisation stores weights in 8 or 4 bits (int8, int4, GGUF formats) cutting memory and often speeding inference with a small quality loss; measure it on your eval, do not assume. Small models excel at narrow, well-specified tasks: classification, extraction, routing, re-ranking. They fail on open-ended reasoning and long instructions, which is where the router escalates.

The pattern that pays: small model first, confidence or a verifier decides, large model on escalation. Evaluate the combined system, because the router's mistakes are the system's mistakes.

entries.title: Multimodal models: images, documents and audio
entries.summary: Vision-capable models read images and page renders directly; use them for layout-heavy documents, and OCR plus text models for bulk text.
entries.body:
Multimodal models accept images (and in some cases audio or video) alongside text. For document work, rendering a PDF page to an image and asking the model to extract fields handles tables, stamps and handwriting that OCR mangles, at a higher token cost per page. For large corpora, a text pipeline (pdf text extraction, layout-aware parsers, OCR for scans) is cheaper and searchable; reserve vision for the pages the text pipeline flags as low quality. Speech-to-text models (Whisper and successors) turn audio into transcripts that then flow through the normal text pipeline.

Evaluate extraction like any other task: a golden set of pages with expected fields and an exact-match score. Images are large in tokens; resize and crop before sending.

entries.title: Scoping an AI project for a client
entries.summary: Map constraints to architecture, define done as numbers on a golden set, deliver in milestones, and hand over something the client can run.
entries.body:
Week one: agree the golden set and a baseline with the client; nothing else is measurable without it. Translate every technology request into an outcome and a metric. Map the constraints (residency, budget, timeline, integration, accuracy tolerance) to an architecture, usually retrieval plus a hosted or EU-hosted model, with fine-tuning parked as a later option. Price a fixed-scope pilot with acceptance criteria (recall, answer quality, abstention, p95, cost per request), a change-control clause, and pass-through model costs with the token arithmetic shown. Put the riskiest unknown first in the plan.

Deliverables: the system in the client's accounts and repo, the eval harness, the runbook with kill switch and rollback, a cost and latency dashboard, an architecture diagram with data flows, and an on-call path. Refuse guarantees of perfection; offer measured targets and a human-review path instead.

entries.title: Observability for LLM applications
entries.summary: Trace every request through retrieval, re-ranking and generation, and log prompt version, model, chunk ids, tokens and cost with the answer.
entries.body:
Without per-request traces you cannot tell a retrieval miss from a generation failure. Log for every answer: request id, user or tenant (pseudonymised), prompt and system-prompt version, model and version, retrieved and re-ranked chunk ids with scores, tokens in and out, latency per stage, cost, finish reason, citation-check result, and any guard that fired. Use OpenTelemetry spans or a dedicated LLM tracing tool. Dashboards: p95 per stage, cost per request, abstention rate, citation failure rate, retry rate, cache hit rate.

Alerts on burn rate against the SLO, on cost per request rising, and on quality proxies (thumbs-down rate, escalations). Sample traces into the golden set. Fail-open paths must emit a typed tag and a counter so silent failures cannot exist.

entries.title: Guardrails, safety layers and human in the loop
entries.summary: Guardrails are code around the model: input checks, output checks, confidence thresholds and a human path for what matters.
entries.body:
Input guardrails: block or route off-topic, abusive or injected inputs, and redact PII. Output guardrails: validate structure, check citations, screen for policy violations, detect refusal loops, and cap length. Confidence: use abstention, self-consistency or a verifier model to decide when to escalate to a human, and make that path fast and logged. High-stakes domains (legal, medical, financial) keep a human approving actions; the model drafts, the person decides.

Guardrails are measured like everything else: false positive and false negative rates on labelled examples, and their latency. A guardrail that silently blocks good answers is a quality bug; log every trip with a reason. The kill switch is the last guardrail and must exist before launch.
